query: Which material can be used for enhance glass-forming ability, and why?

generation.hypothesis: In a multicomponent metallic system that is close to forming a glass (such as a Zr-based bulk metallic glass alloy), a minor addition of a small-atom element (e.g., boron) will enhance the glass‐forming ability by increasing atomic size mismatch and introducing packing frustration that kinetically suppresses crystallization.
generation.material_initial_state: A crystalline or marginally glass–forming multicomponent alloy (e.g., a conventional Zr-based alloy) that under standard cooling rates tends to form coarse crystalline phases.
generation.intervention: Introduce a minor concentration (typically on the order of a few atomic percent) of boron into the base alloy composition.
generation.conditions: Processing under rapid cooling conditions (e.g., melt spinning or suction casting) so that differences in critical cooling rate can be discerned.
generation.structural_mediator: Enhanced atomic size mismatch and local topological disorder due to the small boron atoms disrupting the regular lattice arrangement.
generation.mechanism: Boron atoms, because of their small size, promote local atomic packing frustration and lower atomic mobility. This disrupts the nucleation and growth of crystalline phases during cooling, thereby favoring the formation of an amorphous (glass) structure.
generation.predicted_outcome: The boron–modified alloy will exhibit an increased critical cooling rate (or require a lower cooling rate for glass formation) compared with the base alloy, resulting in a larger composition window and/or thicker samples that form an amorphous phase.
generation.baseline: The unmodified base alloy shows limited glass–forming ability and tends to crystallize upon conventional cooling.
generation.boundary: The beneficial effect is expected only up to an optimum boron concentration; excess boron may trigger formation of boride phases, while very low additions might not sufficiently alter the packing dynamics.
generation.uncertainty: The specific optimal boron content and its quantitative effect on glass forming ability depend strongly on the details of the base alloy composition and processing conditions, and presently there is insufficient direct experimental data in the provided evidence to precisely predict effect magnitudes.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of alloy samples using an identical base Zr-based composition: one set with a small addition (e.g., ~3 at%) of boron and another without. Process both sets using rapid solidification (e.g., melt spinning) under controlled cooling rate conditions and comparable sample thicknesses.
measurements: X-ray diffraction (XRD) to assess the amorphous versus crystalline structure
Differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) to identify glass transition and crystallization exotherms
Transmission electron microscopy (TEM) for microstructural confirmation
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the boron–containing samples exhibit no statistically significant improvement in glass formation (e.g., critical cooling rate reduction, higher glass–forming range, or more pronounced amorphous features in XRD/DSC/TEM measurements) compared to the base alloy, then the hypothesis is falsified.
